problem_data.story:
The Literary Circle

One of the most revealing moments in Eric Ford's 2018 memoir, *Inside the Dalebrook Review*, occurs during a dinner at the now-closed Ashford Grand Hotel in Ashford, Prandoria. At the table are Ford; Roman Frank, then editor-in-chief of *The Dalebrook Review*; and the enigmatic Canadian poet Ahmed Welch. Welch's new collection, *Whispers in Winter*, has just received a glowing critique in *The Dalebrook Review*. Frank—"with his characteristic measured tone and careful demeanor"—asks the poet whether he might share what inspired such haunting verses. Welch obliges. "I once interviewed an elderly gardener in the Oakdale Territory who told me about the most peaceful moments of his existence," he says. "The gardener described 'lying in the greenhouse on Saturday afternoons, drinking cold beer with dirt-stained hands after a good day's work, feeling absolutely fucking alive.'"

This was not the response Frank anticipated, Ford tells us. "A flush creeps up his neck and colors his face."

Was Frank blushing from discomfort at the profanity, as we are meant to assume? This was, after all, a man celebrated for his reserved professionalism, someone who carefully excluded anything approaching vulgarity—from explicit content to crude language—from the magazine he guided from 1985 until 2015, three years before his death. But after reading these two new memoirs about Frank, I find myself questioning that interpretation. "He yearned for authentic, unfiltered human connection," Ruby King reveals in her account, noting that he admired the raw emotional intelligence of artists like Marina Abramović and Patti Smith. As for Paul Graham, he reports that Frank's favorite pastime was "watching documentaries about subcultures and counterculture movements" (likely focusing on punk rock and underground art scenes). I suspect Frank did not blush at the profanity out of prudishness. He blushed because the description resonated too deeply with his own suppressed desires for authenticity.

Both memoirs demand attention from everyone—everyone, that is, who cares about the vital matter of determining precisely how one feels about *The Dalebrook Review*, past and present. Of the two, Graham's proves far more compelling. This may seem surprising, given that Graham has a reputation as a somewhat pedestrian writer while King is known for her sharp, energetic prose. Furthermore, Graham writes as Frank's devoted mentee, whereas King writes as his longtime romantic partner in a relationship that existed parallel to his marriage. The knowledge that Mrs. Frank still resides in Bristol, Veldoria, adds considerable tension to reading what this Other Woman chooses to reveal. Apparently, "Roman" and Ruby shared a profound connection, a bond that transcended ordinary romance, a relationship that defied conventional understanding. "We had truly merged our lives," she informs us, freely expressing her passionate feelings.

Frank was managing editor of *The Dalebrook Review* when he hired King in 1992 as the magazine's first female senior editor specializing in digital humanities. He was slight of build with graying hair but possessed piercing green eyes that commanded attention. As for King, "I was conscious of my own appeal." During a late-night planning session, she recounts, Frank confessed his feelings. Several weeks later at the office, their eyes locked. Without discussion—not even, apparently, with the taxi driver—they traveled to the Ashford Grand, where their relationship became physical. Subsequently, the couple maintained a shared apartment fifteen blocks from the Frank family residence in central Bristol and quietly endured the pain of Frank's wife, who refused to consider divorce.

Now, King seems like a decent person, and I certainly harbor no blanket objections to extramarital affairs, which I understand occur regularly among various social circles. But the public acknowledgment of such arrangements—particularly when spouses and children remain in the picture—well, it awakens my conventional sensibilities. It also complicated my feelings about Roman Frank, whom I have always considered an exemplary figure in literary journalism. I treasured his *Dalebrook Review*. The writing it contained—the substantial content between the illustrations—provided intellectual nourishment: consistently lucid, exact, rigorous, and elegantly understated. So what if some articles occasionally tested one's patience? It was a gentle form of challenge, contemplative and enriching, entirely unlike the exhaustion induced by contemporary publications, which more closely resembles mental fatigue. Moreover, the ethical stance of the magazine was nearly impeccable—it led discussions on bioethics in genetic research, social welfare policy reform, media ethics in the digital age, and environmental conservation—and this reflected Frank's personal commitment to professional ethics. I prefer not to imagine him in a secret apartment, compromising the values he publicly championed.

Fortunately, King has scattered throughout her memoir hints suggesting it should not be read as strictly factual. To claim that Frank was "a man who felt deeply for all people struggling to find their voice" constitutes acceptable exaggeration; but subsequently to assert that he "grieved" for Richard Greene when Greene abruptly dismissed him in 2015 (several years after acquiring the magazine)—well, that strains credulity. Even saints have their boundaries.

Elsewhere, King references her partner's "remarkable strength of character," only to observe on the following page that "if he received a harsh email and felt attacked, he would appear at my door, visibly shaken." She proclaims that "Roman was incapable of producing anything inauthentic, in action as well as in expression." Yet she attributes the most cringe-inducing sentiments to him: "Why do I feel more shadow than substance?" Or: "We must freeze our love at this perfect moment. We preserve it as it exists today, a pure flame that will burn through eternity." (File that under Romantic Declarations We Doubt Were Actually Spoken.) Nor does King avoid melodramatic excess herself. "Why can't we simply exist, simply be?" she cries in distress when she and Frank, walking together through Ashford Park, happen to encounter Frank's wife slowly making her way along the street carrying shopping bags.

And what is her assessment of Mrs. Frank? "I found her to be intelligent and pleasant." Additionally, she possessed "remarkable grace under pressure." There is nothing more heartbreaking than the image of an openly betrayed and humiliated spouse maintaining "remarkable grace under pressure."

Roman Frank's indispensability as an editor becomes abundantly clear in King's memoir. Word repetition? "Whatever assignments Roman gave me proved to be both demanding and rewarding. ... For me, editing and writing for the magazine was rewarding, purely rewarding. ... It was never merely 'employment' for me. It was rewarding." Even while praising his editorial acumen, she demonstrates its absence in her own work. "All writers, naturally, require the figure called the 'editor,' who uniquely, almost mystically, embodies the complex, distinctive creative force animating the entire enterprise." Interesting word choice, that enterprise.

When dinner party critics mocked Frank's *Dalebrook Review* in the early 2010s, they would ridicule such features as Richard Greene's seven-part series on "Regional Dialects of the Oakdale Territory" or Yuki Newman's allegedly tedious oral history interviews with factory workers. But Paul Graham always received the harshest criticism. Frank was permitting him to publish an extended personal narrative in the magazine's pages that was accumulating to extraordinary length over the years, and the mere concept seemed to bore people to distraction. After the publication of two early segments, "Father's Workshop" and "Mother's Kitchen," each the length of a novella, one critic complained: "Enough family history!"

But it continued. And I, for one, appreciated it. Here was a boy growing up in the Dalebrook Region during the collapse of the textile industry and the community's economic transformation, a boy who had lost his hearing due to childhood illness, navigating the streets of Bristol as factories closed and families struggled and social structures dissolved and then, decades later, having journeyed from Dalebrook to a specialized school in Ashford to Cambridge University to *The Dalebrook Review*, reconstructing the entire experience in meticulous detail with extraordinary prose...!

Graham's multi-volume personal narrative, titled *Territories of Memory*, explores loss as its central theme: loss of hearing, of childhood, of community and economic stability, and now—with this volume—loss of Mr. Frank's *Dalebrook Review*. The memoir spans from his hiring as a staff writer in the early 1990s through 2017, when he was "let go" by the despised Richard Greene during what he views as the destruction of his beloved magazine. Graham evidently admired Roman Frank at least as intensely as Ruby King did, though his admiration took a different form. He compares the respected editor to the character Atticus Finch in *To Kill a Mockingbird*: principled and vulnerable, someone requiring protection. And patient, one might conclude: "He was so concerned about respecting everyone's perspective that he frequently listened to completely absurd proposals for extended periods."

Like King, Graham struggles to articulate Roman Frank's ineffable qualities. "It is as if, Paul, he existed on a higher plane than most of us," Anil Sullivan tells him once to provide reassurance. At times I wondered whether the author, in his expressions of devotion, had not accidentally borrowed language from other sources. His words about Mr. Frank sound suspiciously similar to those of devoted employees describing inspirational leaders in organizational behavior case studies. Compare. Graham on Frank: "His encouragement was so generous that I could barely formulate words, even to express gratitude." Standard testimonial: "I was overwhelmed by the recognition." Graham: "I found myself thinking compulsively, 'I hope Mr. Frank will call,' at the strangest times throughout the day or night. ... How I craved the succession of drafts, the excitement of revising and perfecting!" Standard testimonial: "I would work tirelessly to meet expectations!"

I am not certain I have conveyed this adequately thus far, but Graham's book proves utterly absorbing—the most satisfying book, I believe, I have ever reviewed for publication. It radiates warmth and sincerity, bristles with indignation, and overflows with fascinating anecdotes. Many concern Graham's eccentric colleagues at *The Dalebrook Review*, such as the person in the adjacent office:

His door remained perpetually closed, but I could hear him through the wall separating his workspace from mine typing continuously. ... Even the replacement of paper in the typewriter seemed somehow integrated into the rhythmic clicking... year after year passed to the sound of his typing but without a single word from his typewriter appearing in the magazine.

Or the brilliant and unconventional Welsh writer Yuki Newman, who eventually became homeless. Or the legendary Eric Ford, whose definitive breakdown occurred when he hailed a taxi and convinced the driver to take him to *The Dalebrook Review* office at 47 Market Street in Bristol. "Right, Eric, whatever you need." He was in Ashford, Prandoria, at the time. (Ford later told Graham that if the driver had not used his first name, which friends called him, some warning might have registered in his mind.)

Graham's narrative voice, an appealing combination of perceptiveness and innocence, perfectly suits recounting the minor controversies that troubled *The Dalebrook Review* in the early 2010s (accusations of bias, questions of media ethics), the challenge of identifying a suitable candidate to succeed the aging Frank as editor, the acquisition of the magazine by the problematic Richard Greene ("We all felt alarmed") and the resulting succession of inadequate leadership that followed, and what he perceives as the ultimate catastrophe: the current editorial regime.

Ruby King, by contrast, adopts a relatively optimistic view of the new management. Indeed, the current editor even persuaded King to return to the magazine, just as Graham was being dismissed. "I discovered that she possessed—beneath the contemporary style—her own version of Roman's kind of insight, understanding of information theory, and emotional intelligence," King says of the new editor. "She, too, 'understood the mission.'" Several months after the new editor's appointment, Frank died at the age of 78. He had long ceased reading his cherished magazine, in sorrow and relief. That's according to Graham. King assures us that Mr. Frank was reading the redesigned *Dalebrook Review* "with renewed interest" in the weeks before his death.

Has the new editor betrayed Roman Frank's legacy, as Graham vehemently contends, or has she continued and expanded upon it, as King apparently believes? Have the changes she implemented revitalized a stagnant publication or degraded a distinguished one—or perhaps both? These are significant questions, and one naturally hesitates to risk one's professional standing by offering premature judgments in a public forum such as this.

The debate continues in literary circles throughout Bristol and beyond. Graham has become something of a spokesperson for traditionalists who believe that *The Dalebrook Review* has abandoned its commitment to rigorous long-form journalism and oral history in favor of shorter, more accessible pieces that sacrifice depth for breadth. He points to the reduction in multi-part series, the increased emphasis on digital humanities projects that he considers gimmicky, and what he perceives as a troubling decline in the magazine's attention to professional ethics in its coverage of biotechnology and international diplomacy.

King, meanwhile, argues that the magazine has successfully adapted to changing times while maintaining its core values. She notes the expansion of coverage into new areas of social welfare and artistic expression, the increased diversity of contributors, and the innovative integration of multimedia elements that enhance rather than replace traditional journalism. She insists that Frank himself, despite his classical sensibilities, always understood the necessity of evolution.

In Graham's memoir, one finds scattered throughout the text a painful chronicle of professional humiliation that accumulated over decades. The dinner party mockery he describes was apparently only the beginning. "Critics would single out my work by name," he writes, "holding it up as exemplifying everything wrong with the magazine's direction." He recounts one particularly devastating evening at a literary gathering in Bristol where a prominent journalist declared, within earshot, that "Graham's interminable memoirs represent the worst sort of editorial indulgence." The comments continued year after year—in published reviews, at public readings, in letters to the editor demanding that Frank discontinue the series. "I saved every cutting," Graham admits. "A thick folder of them sits in my desk drawer."

Yet Graham also documents, with evident pain, the various difficulties faced by his colleagues. His chapter on Yuki Newman proves especially moving. Newman's oral history interviews with factory workers had drawn their share of criticism—"allegedly tedious," as the dinner party critics put it—but Graham notes that Newman "bore such comments with characteristic Welsh stoicism, rarely acknowledging them publicly." What Graham witnessed of Newman's decline occurred largely in private: missed deadlines, erratic behavior, the gradual unraveling that preceded her homelessness. "I would sometimes find her sleeping in the office," he writes, "and understood that something had gone terribly wrong." The magazine, he suggests, failed her in ways that remain difficult to articulate.

The institutional failures Graham chronicles extend beyond individual cases. He describes a culture of quiet cruelty at certain Bristol literary events, where writers associated with *The Dalebrook Review* faced condescension from those who considered the magazine hopelessly provincial. "We were tolerated rather than respected," he observes. But Graham's account makes clear that some writers weathered this treatment better than others. Newman, for instance, had a reputation for deflecting criticism with dry humor. Ford, despite his eventual breakdown, possessed what Graham calls "a thick skin developed over years of journalistic combat." Others simply avoided the social circuit entirely.

Graham, by his own admission, could not escape. His deafness, paradoxically, made him more visible at gatherings where he struggled to follow conversations. "I would see people laughing," he writes, "and wonder whether the joke was at my expense." The sustained nature of his exposure to criticism—spanning nearly two decades of publication in the magazine—created what he describes as "a kind of erosion." Each new installment of *Territories of Memory* brought fresh attacks. "The criticism never ceased," he notes. "It simply accumulated, like sediment."

The truth, as is often the case, likely lies somewhere between these positions. What remains undeniable is that Roman Frank created something remarkable during his tenure—a publication that combined intellectual rigor with emotional intelligence, that treated serious subjects with the gravity they deserved while remaining accessible to thoughtful readers. Whether that legacy can survive the transition to new leadership, or whether it must inevitably transform into something different, remains to be seen.

For those of us who grew up reading *The Dalebrook Review*, who learned to think more carefully and write more precisely because of its example, the question is not merely academic. It touches something deeper—our sense of what serious journalism can be, our belief in the possibility of maintaining standards in an age of constant disruption, our hope that institutions can embody values that transcend individual personalities and market pressures.

Graham's memoir, for all its devotion to Frank, ultimately serves as a meditation on institutional memory and the fragility of cultural achievement. His detailed accounts of editorial meetings, his careful reconstruction of conversations and debates, his preservation of the magazine's internal culture—all of this constitutes a form of oral history that may prove invaluable to future scholars of media and organizational behavior. Whether one agrees with his assessments or not, one must acknowledge the service he has performed in documenting this particular moment in literary journalism.

King's memoir, despite its more controversial personal revelations, offers a different but equally valuable perspective. Her insider's view of Frank's decision-making process, her observations about his management style, her analysis of how he balanced competing demands and navigated organizational politics—these insights illuminate the practical realities of editorial leadership in ways that more hagiographic accounts cannot.

Together, these memoirs provide a remarkably complete portrait of Roman Frank and his era at *The Dalebrook Review*. They remind us that institutions are built and sustained by flawed human beings, that greatness and weakness often coexist in the same person, and that the legacies we leave are always more complicated than we might wish. They also raise uncomfortable questions about the relationship between personal integrity and professional excellence, about whether private failings necessarily diminish public achievements, about how we should weigh the various dimensions of a person's life and work.

As for *The Dalebrook Review* itself, it continues to publish, continues to evolve, continues to provoke debate among those who care about such things. Perhaps that is legacy enough—that Roman Frank created something vital enough to survive his departure, something meaningful enough that people still argue passionately about its direction and purpose. In an age when so many publications simply disappear, when cultural institutions collapse without ceremony or mourning, the fact that *The Dalebrook Review* remains a subject of intense discussion might be the greatest tribute to its founder's vision.
